newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil arrests 11 as army clears blocked gold mine.
newsitem.headline: Brazil arrests 11 as army clears blocked gold mine.

text.p: Brazil sent federal police and troops on Thursday to remove wildcat gold-diggers from a huge Amazon gold deposit, arresting 11 people in an operation that officials said passed without bloodshed.

Justice Minister Nelson Jobim said about 60 Federal Police officers backed by about 300 soldiers cleared a road leading to Serra Leste in the northern state of Para, a gold field which lies near the site of the largest gold rush in history.
"The operation was a success. There wasn't a single injury nor any resistance," Jobim told reporters, adding that police were still hunting some people who escaped the dragnet.

Hundreds of "garimpeiros", as freelance gold prospectors are called in Portuguese, have succeeded in blocking survey work at Serra Leste since May, causing state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) up to $10 million in losses.
The deposit is thought to contain about 150 tons of the precious metal, buried deep beneath the soil.

The garimpeiros claim a share of the profits because it lies near the Serra Pelada gold mine, where at their peak in 1988, up to one million freelance prospectors produced 90 tons out of Brazil's total gold production of 113 tons.
Serra Pelada was made famous by the "human anthill" images of Brazilian photographer Sebastiao Salgado, showing thousands of garimpeiros lugging baskets of rocks up precarious ladders.

Once the world's largest opencast mine, Serra Pelada is now a memorial to those who died in the malaria-invested jungle. The discovery in February of another massive gold deposit at nearby Serra Leste revived their dreams of overnight fortunes.

Jobim said Brasilia had obeyed a judicial order in clearing the area. He said the operation had nothing to do with CVRD's impending privatisation and the potential impact the Serra Leste gold could have on its market value.
He said a core of some 60 protesters had blocked the mine, demanding tolls from people and damaging equipment. He said about 16 ringleaders were likely to be prosecuted.
Federal deputy Antonio Feijao, who headed a probe of claims to the Serra Leste gold, said most of the 1,900 garimpeiro families in the area backed the joint police-army operation.

"But if the government doesn't follow up with dialogue, then we'll have a situation like we have with the Yanomami Indians (on the border with Venezuela)," Feijao told Reuters. "The garimpeiros will leave for a while and then go back."
Despite claims most locals backed the eviction, garimpeiro leaders attacked the use of force before it had even happened.
Jose Antonio Machado, head of the garimpeiros union, wrote in Thursday's Correio Braziliense newspaper that the cost of sending in the army to clear out the squatters would be high.

Taking a jibe at the social-democrat credentials of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, a sociology professor turned head of government, Machado said Cardoso would never have used the armed forces against helpless miners in the past.
"When he was still a presidential candidate, he would never have taken by force this filthy gold mine, whose exploration will cost even more if tainted with injuries," he said.
